1	# ORC Runtime Design
2	
3	The ORC runtime provides APIs for *executor* processes in an ORC JIT session
4	(as opposed to the LLVM ORC libraries which provide APIs for *controller*
5	processes). This includes support for both JIT'd code itself, and for users
6	of JIT'd code.
7	
8	## Background
9	
10	LLVM's On Request Compilation (ORC) APIs support cross-process loading of JIT'd
11	code. We call the process that defines and links the JIT'd code the *controller*
12	and the process that executes JIT'd code the *executor*. Controller processes
13	will link LLVM's ORC library, and construct a JIT'd program using an
14	llvm::orc::ExecutionSession instance (typically through an convenience wrapper
15	like llvm::orc::LLJIT). Executor processes construct an `orc_rt::Session`
16	object to manage resources for, and access to, JIT'd code within the executor
17	process.
18	
19	## APIs
20	
21	### Session
22	
23	The Session object is the root object for a JIT'd program. It owns the
24	Service instances that manage services and resources supporting JIT'd code
25	(e.g. JIT'd memory, unwind info registrations, dynamic library handles, etc.).
26	
27	The Session object must be constructed prior to adding any JIT'd code, and must
28	outlive execution of any JIT'd code.
29	
30	An executor may have more than one Session object, in which case each Session
31	object must outlive execution of any JIT'd code added to that specific session.
32	
33	### ControllerAccess
34	
35	ControllerAccess objects support bidirectional RPC between JIT'd code in the
36	executor and the ExecutionSession in the controller.
37	
38	Calls in both directions are to "wrapper functions" with a fixed signature (a
39	function that takes a blob of bytes and returns a blob of bytes as its result).
40	ControllerAccess objects can not generally assume anything about the format of
41	the bytes being sent (their interpretation is up to the called function). The
42	RPC is not fully symmetric: Calls from the controller to the executor specify
43	wrapper function *addresses* (i.e. the controller can invoke any code in the
44	executor). Calls from the executor to the controller specify *tags*, which are
45	addresses in the executor processes that are associated with handlers in the
46	controller. This ensures that the executing process can only call deliberately
47	exposed entry points in the controller.
48	
49	ControllerAccess objects may be detached before the session ends, at which point
50	JIT'd code may continue executing, but will receive no further calls from the
51	controller and can make no further calls to the controller.
52	
53	### Service
54	
55	`Service` is an interface for classes that provide services to the Session.
56	E.g. memory managers, or dynamic library loaders.
57	
58	The `Service` interface provides two operations: `onDetach` and `onShutdown`.
59	`onDetach` signals that controller access is permanently unavailable. It is
60	always called before `onShutdown`, regardless of how the Session reaches
61	shutdown -- including when no controller was ever attached. Since no further
62	requests will be made by the controller after `onDetach`, Services may use it
63	to abandon any fine-grained book-keeping that is only needed to service
64	controller requests. Many Services will implement `onDetach` as a no-op.
65	
66	The `onShutdown` operation will be called at `Session` destruction time, after
67	all in-flight managed code calls have completed. Services should release all
68	held resources during `onShutdown`.
69	
70	### Managed code execution and shutdown
71	
72	Session teardown must not proceed while JIT'd code is still live on a stack:
73	freeing the JIT'd code (and the resources it runs against) out from under those
74	frames would crash the moment control returns to them.
75	
76	To help enforce this the Session carries a managed-code `TaskGroup`. Code that
77	is about to run JIT'd code obtains a `TaskGroup::Token` from the group to
78	bracket that execution, and the group delays Session shutdown until every Token
79	has been released. `Session::callManagedCode` acquires and holds a Token for you
80	around a synchronous call; Tokens can also be acquired manually from the
81	`TokenSource` returned by `Session::managedCodeTokenSource`.
82	
83	A Token brackets a single span of execution on a stack -- *not* a whole chain of
84	asynchronous operations. When an asynchronous operation captures a continuation,
85	whoever later invokes that continuation must obtain a fresh Token to bracket the
86	invocation (the continuation can't do it itself: its entry point may already be
87	JIT'd code).
88	
89	Token acquisition fails once Session shutdown has been requested -- and it can
90	fail even for a nested or resumed call whose caller already holds a Token. So
91	every caller of JIT'd code needs a way to abort and unwind when acquisition is
92	denied; `callManagedCode` reports denial through its return value, which callers
93	must check.
94	
95	### TaskDispatcher
96	
97	Runs Tasks within the ORC runtime. In particular, calls originating from the
98	controller (via ControllerAccess) will be dispatched as Tasks.
99	
100	TaskDispatchers are responsible for ensuring that all dispatched Tasks have
101	completed or been destroyed during Session shutdown.
102	
103	### WrapperFunction
104	
105	A wrapper function is any function with the following C signature:
106	
107	```c
108	void (orc_rt_SessionRef Session, uint64_t CallId,
109	      orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn Return,
110	      orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer ArgBytes);
111	```
112	
113	where `orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn` and `orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer` are
114	defined as:
115	
116	```c
117	typedef struct {
118	  orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBufferDataUnion Data;
119	  size_t Size;
120	} orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer;
121	
122	/**
123	 * Asynchronous return function for an orc-rt wrapper function.
124	 */
125	typedef void (*orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn)(
126	    orc_rt_SessionRef Session, uint64_t CallId,
127	    orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer ResultBytes);
128	```
129	
130	The orc_rt::WrapperFunction class provides APIs for implementing and calling
131	wrapper functions.
132	
133	### SPSWrapperFunction
134	
135	An SPS wrapper function is a wrapper function that uses the
136	SimplePackedSerialization scheme (see documentation in
137	orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SimplePackedSerialization.h).
138	
139	## TODO:
140	
141	Document...
142	
143	* C API
144	* Error handling
145	* RTTI
146	* ExecutorAddr / ExecutorAddrRange
147	* SimpleNativeMemoryMap
148	* Memory Access (unimplemented)
149	* Platform classes (unimplemented)
150	* Other utilities

llvm::orc::ExecutionSession instance (typically through an convenience wrapper
like llvm::orc::LLJIT). Executor processes construct an `orc_rt::Session`
object to manage resources for, and access to, JIT'd code within the executor
process.

## APIs

### Session

The Session object is the root object for a JIT'd program. It owns the
Service instances that manage services and resources supporting JIT'd code
(e.g. JIT'd memory, unwind info registrations, dynamic library handles, etc.).

The Session object must be constructed prior to adding any JIT'd code, and must
outlive execution of any JIT'd code.

An executor may have more than one Session object, in which case each Session
object must outlive execution of any JIT'd code added to that specific session.

### ControllerAccess

ControllerAccess objects support bidirectional RPC between JIT'd code in the
executor and the ExecutionSession in the controller.

Calls in both directions are to "wrapper functions" with a fixed signature (a
function that takes a blob of bytes and returns a blob of bytes as its result).
ControllerAccess objects can not generally assume anything about the format of
the bytes being sent (their interpretation is up to the called function). The
RPC is not fully symmetric: Calls from the controller to the executor specify
wrapper function *addresses* (i.e. the controller can invoke any code in the
executor). Calls from the executor to the controller specify *tags*, which are
addresses in the executor processes that are associated with handlers in the
controller. This ensures that the executing process can only call deliberately
exposed entry points in the controller.

ControllerAccess objects may be detached before the session ends, at which point
JIT'd code may continue executing, but will receive no further calls from the
controller and can make no further calls to the controller.

### Service

`Service` is an interface for classes that provide services to the Session.
E.g. memory managers, or dynamic library loaders.

The `Service` interface provides two operations: `onDetach` and `onShutdown`.
`onDetach` signals that controller access is permanently unavailable. It is
always called before `onShutdown`, regardless of how the Session reaches
shutdown -- including when no controller was ever attached. Since no further
requests will be made by the controller after `onDetach`, Services may use it
to abandon any fine-grained book-keeping that is only needed to service
controller requests. Many Services will implement `onDetach` as a no-op.

The `onShutdown` operation will be called at `Session` destruction time, after
all in-flight managed code calls have completed. Services should release all
held resources during `onShutdown`.

### Managed code execution and shutdown

Session teardown must not proceed while JIT'd code is still live on a stack:
freeing the JIT'd code (and the resources it runs against) out from under those
frames would crash the moment control returns to them.

To help enforce this the Session carries a managed-code `TaskGroup`. Code that
is about to run JIT'd code obtains a `TaskGroup::Token` from the group to
bracket that execution, and the group delays Session shutdown until every Token
has been released. `Session::callManagedCode` acquires and holds a Token for you
around a synchronous call; Tokens can also be acquired manually from the
`TokenSource` returned by `Session::managedCodeTokenSource`.

A Token brackets a single span of execution on a stack -- *not* a whole chain of
asynchronous operations. When an asynchronous operation captures a continuation,
whoever later invokes that continuation must obtain a fresh Token to bracket the
invocation (the continuation can't do it itself: its entry point may already be
JIT'd code).

Token acquisition fails once Session shutdown has been requested -- and it can
fail even for a nested or resumed call whose caller already holds a Token. So
every caller of JIT'd code needs a way to abort and unwind when acquisition is
denied; `callManagedCode` reports denial through its return value, which callers
must check.

### TaskDispatcher

Runs Tasks within the ORC runtime. In particular, calls originating from the
controller (via ControllerAccess) will be dispatched as Tasks.

TaskDispatchers are responsible for ensuring that all dispatched Tasks have
completed or been destroyed during Session shutdown.

### WrapperFunction

A wrapper function is any function with the following C signature:

```c
void (orc_rt_SessionRef Session, uint64_t CallId,
      orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn Return,
      orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer ArgBytes);
```

where `orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn` and `orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer` are
defined as:

```c
typedef struct {
  orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBufferDataUnion Data;
  size_t Size;
} orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer;

/**
 * Asynchronous return function for an orc-rt wrapper function.
 */
typedef void (*orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn)(
    orc_rt_SessionRef Session, uint64_t CallId,
    orc_rt_WrapperFunctionBuffer ResultBytes);
```

The orc_rt::WrapperFunction class provides APIs for implementing and calling
wrapper functions.

### SPSWrapperFunction

An SPS wrapper function is a wrapper function that uses the
SimplePackedSerialization scheme (see documentation in
orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SimplePackedSerialization.h).

# LLVM ORC Runtime

## Overview

The ORC runtime provides executor-side support code for the LLVM ORC APIs.

```{eval-rst}
.. toctree::
   :titlesonly:

   Building-orc-rt
   CodingConventions
```

### Current Status

The ORC Runtime is a new, experimental project. It is being actively developed,
and neither the ABI nor API are stable. LLVM ORC API clients should be careful
to use an ORC Runtime from the same build as their LLVM ORC libraries.

### Platform and Compiler Support

* Clang 16 and above

2	
3	## Getting Started
4	
5	The basic steps needed to build orc-rt are:
6	
7	* Checkout llvm-project:
8	
9	   * ``cd where-you-want-llvm-to-live``
10	   * ``git clone https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project.git``
11	
12	* Configure and build orc-rt:
13	
14	   CMake is the only supported configuration system.
15	
16	   Clang is the preferred compiler when building and using orc-rt.
17	
18	   * ``cd where you want to build llvm``
19	   * ``mkdir build``
20	   * ``cd build``
21	   * ``cmake -G <generator> -DLLVM_ENABLE_RUNTIMES=orc-rt [options] <llvm-monorepo>/runtimes``
22	
23	   For more information about configuring orc-rt see :ref:`CMake Options`.
24	
25	   * ``make orc-rt`` --- will build orc-rt.
26	   * ``make check-orc-rt`` --- will run the test suite.
27	
28	   Shared and static libraries for orc-rt should now be present in
29	   llvm/build/lib.
30	
31	* **Optional**: Install orc-rt
32	
33	   Remember to use the CMake option ``CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX`` to select a safe
34	   place to install orc-rt.
35	
36	   * ``make install-orc-rt`` --- Will install the libraries and the headers
37	
38	## CMake Options
39	
40	Here are some of the CMake variables that are used often, along with a
41	brief explanation and LLVM-specific notes. For full documentation, check the
42	CMake docs or execute ``cmake --help-variable VARIABLE_NAME``.
43	
44	**CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE**:STRING
45	  Sets the build type for ``make`` based generators. Possible values are
46	  Release, Debug, RelWithDebInfo and MinSizeRel. On systems like Visual Studio
47	  the user sets the build type with the IDE settings.
48	
49	**CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX**:PATH
50	  Path where LLVM will be installed if "make install" is invoked or the
51	  "INSTALL" target is built.
52	
53	**CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER**:STRING
54	  The C++ compiler to use when building and testing orc-rt.
55	
56	## orc-rt specific options
57	
58	* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS:BOOL
59	
60	  **Default**: ``ON``
61	
62	  Toggle assertions independent of the build mode.
63	
64	* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_PEDANTIC:BOOL
65	
66	  **Default**: ``ON``
67	
68	  Compile with -Wpedantic.
69	
70	* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_WERROR:BOOL

72	  **Default**: ``ON``

   * ``cd where-you-want-llvm-to-live``
   * ``git clone https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project.git``

* Configure and build orc-rt:

   CMake is the only supported configuration system.

   Clang is the preferred compiler when building and using orc-rt.

   * ``cd where you want to build llvm``
   * ``mkdir build``
   * ``cd build``
   * ``cmake -G <generator> -DLLVM_ENABLE_RUNTIMES=orc-rt [options] <llvm-monorepo>/runtimes``

   For more information about configuring orc-rt see :ref:`CMake Options`.

   * ``make orc-rt`` --- will build orc-rt.
   * ``make check-orc-rt`` --- will run the test suite.

   Shared and static libraries for orc-rt should now be present in
   llvm/build/lib.

* **Optional**: Install orc-rt

   Remember to use the CMake option ``CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX`` to select a safe
   place to install orc-rt.

   * ``make install-orc-rt`` --- Will install the libraries and the headers

## CMake Options

Here are some of the CMake variables that are used often, along with a
brief explanation and LLVM-specific notes. For full documentation, check the
CMake docs or execute ``cmake --help-variable VARIABLE_NAME``.

**CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE**:STRING
  Sets the build type for ``make`` based generators. Possible values are
  Release, Debug, RelWithDebInfo and MinSizeRel. On systems like Visual Studio
  the user sets the build type with the IDE settings.

**CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX**:PATH
  Path where LLVM will be installed if "make install" is invoked or the
  "INSTALL" target is built.

**CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER**:STRING
  The C++ compiler to use when building and testing orc-rt.

## orc-rt specific options

* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS:BOOL

  **Default**: ``ON``

  Toggle assertions independent of the build mode.

* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_PEDANTIC:BOOL

  **Default**: ``ON``

  Compile with -Wpedantic.

* option:: ORC_RT_ENABLE_WERROR:BOOL

  **Default**: ``ON``

  Compile with -Werror

1	# ORC-RT Error Handling Policy
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	ORC-RT uses a structured error handling system based on the `orc_rt::Error` and
6	`orc_rt::Expected<T>` classes. This system provides type-safe error propagation
7	that works consistently across different compilation configurations (with or
8	without C++ exceptions).
9	
10	## Fundamental Principles
11	
12	### 1. Error Representation
13	- **Success**: Represented by `Error::success()` - a lightweight, zero-cost value
14	- **Failure**: Represented by `Error` objects containing typed error information
15	- **Values with Potential Errors**: Use `Expected<T>` to combine success values
16	  with error handling
17	
18	### 2. Error Categories
19	
20	**Recoverable Errors**: Environmental issues that can be handled gracefully
21	- File I/O failures, network issues, malformed input
22	- Use `Error` and `Expected<T>` return types
23	- Examples: `StringError`, `MyCustomError`
24	
25	**Programmatic Errors**: Violations of API contracts or program invariants
26	- Use assertions
27	- Should terminate the program immediately
28	- Examples: Unexpected null pointers, invalid enum values
29	
30	> **Important: Library Design Principles**
31	>
32	> **ORC-RT is a library and must never call terminating functions** like `exit()`,
33	> `abort()`, or `std::terminate()` in response to recoverable errors. Libraries
34	> should always return errors to their callers, allowing the application to decide
35	> how to handle them.
36	
37	## Core Error Types
38	
39	### Error
40	```cpp
41	namespace orc_rt {
42	  class Error {
43	  public:
44	    // Create success value
45	    static Error success();
46	
47	    // Check for failure
48	    explicit operator bool();  // true = failure, false = success
49	
50	    // Type checking
51	    template<typename ErrT> bool isA() const;
52	
53	    // Exception interop (when exceptions enabled)
54	    void throwOnFailure();
55	  };
56	}
57	```
58	
59	### Expected<T>
60	```cpp
61	template<typename T>
62	class Expected {
63	public:
64	  // Construction
65	  Expected(T Value);
66	  Expected(Error Err);
67	
68	  // Check for success
69	  explicit operator bool();  // true = success, false = failure
70	
71	  // Access value (success case)
72	  T& operator*();
73	  T* operator->();
74	
75	  // Extract error (failure case)
76	  Error takeError();
77	};
78	```
79	
80	## Defining Custom Error Types
81	
82	Use `ErrorExtends<ThisT, ParentT>`:
83	
84	```cpp
85	class CustomError : public ErrorExtends<CustomError, ErrorInfoBase> {
86	public:
87	  CustomError(std::string Message) : Message(std::move(Message)) {}
88	
89	  std::string toString() const noexcept override {
90	    return "CustomError: " + Message;
91	  }
92	
93	  const std::string& getMessage() const { return Message; }
94	
95	private:
96	  std::string Message;
97	};
98	
99	// Usage
100	Error doSomething() {
101	  if (/* error condition */)
102	    return make_error<CustomError>("Something went wrong");
103	  return Error::success();
104	}
105	```
106	
107	## Error Handling Patterns
108	
109	### Basic Error Propagation
110	```cpp
111	Error processFile(StringRef Path) {
112	  if (auto Err = openFile(Path))
113	    return Err;  // Propagate error
114	
115	  if (auto Err = validateFormat(Path))
116	    return Err;
117	
118	  return Error::success();
119	}
120	```
121	
122	### Expected<T> Usage
123	```cpp
124	Expected<Data> loadData(StringRef Path) {
125	  auto FileOrErr = openFile(Path);
126	  if (auto Err = FileOrErr.takeError())
127	    return Err;
128	
129	  return parseData(*FileOrErr);
130	}
131	
132	// Alternative form
133	Expected<Data> loadData(StringRef Path) {
134	  if (auto FileOrErr = openFile(Path)) {
135	    auto& File = *FileOrErr;
136	    return parseData(File);
137	  } else {
138	    return FileOrErr.takeError();
139	  }
140	}
141	```
142	
143	### Error Consumption
144	Error values are most commonly passed up the stack (having interrupted whatever
145	operation raised the error). Eventually errors must be consumed (failure to do
146	so will trigger an assertion). Errors may be consumed using one of the
147	following patterns:
148	
149	```cpp
150	// 1. Handle specific error types
151	handleAllErrors(mayFail(),
152	  [](const CustomError& CE) {
153	    // Handle CustomError
154	  },
155	  [](ErrorInfoBase& EIB) {
156	    // Handle any other error
157	  }
158	);
159	
160	// 2. Report errors to the Session:
161	//    This should be done for Errors that cannot be passed further up the stack
162	//    (e.g. the have reached the root of some thread)
163	{
164	  if (auto Err = mayFail())
165	    S.reportError(std::move(Err));
166	  // thread ends here.
167	}
168	
169	// 3. Convert to string and log:
170	//    This option may be used in contexts where a reference to the Session is
171	//    not available.
172	logError(toString(mayFail()));
173	
174	// 4  Consume and ignore (explicit)
175	//    Errors can be explicitly consumed in cases where a failure is known to be
176	//    benign.
177	if (auto Err = tryPopulateFromOnDiskCache(...))
178	  consumeError(std::move(Err)); // Error indicates cache unavailable. Benign.
179	```
180	
181	## Exception Interoperability
182	
183	When `ORC_RT_ENABLE_EXCEPTIONS=On`, ORC-RT provides bidirectional conversion
184	between errors and exceptions.
185	
186	> **Important: Exception Usage Policy**
187	>
188	> **ORC-RT should not use exceptions internally.** All ORC-RT functions should
189	> use `Error` and `Expected<T>` return types for error reporting. Exceptions
190	> should only be used at the boundaries:
191	>
192	> 1. **Converting external exceptions to errors** when calling
193	>      exception-throwing external code
194	> 2. **Converting errors to exceptions** when returning from ORC-RT to
195	>      exception-expecting client code
196	>
197	> This policy ensures that:
198	> - ORC-RT works consistently whether exceptions are enabled or disabled
199	> - Error handling behavior is predictable and doesn't depend on exception
200	>   propagation
201	> - The library remains compatible with codebases that disable exceptions
202	>   (most LLVM projects)
203	
204	### Core Interop APIs
205	
206	**`runCapturingExceptions`**: Converts exceptions to errors
207	```cpp
208	// Return type depends on callback:
209	//   void        → Error
210	//   Error       → Error
211	//   Expected<T> → Expected<T>
212	//   T           → Expected<T>
213	
214	auto Result = runCapturingExceptions([]() {
215	  return riskyOperation();  // might throw
216	});
217	```
218	
219	**`Error::throwOnFailure`**: Converts errors to exceptions
220	```cpp
221	try {
222	  auto Err = orcOperation();
223	  Err.throwOnFailure();  // Throws if Err represents failure
224	} catch (std::unique_ptr<StringError>& E) {
225	  // Catch specific error types
226	} catch (std::unique_ptr<ErrorInfoBase>& E) {
227	  // Catch any ORC error
228	} catch (...) {
229	  // Catch other exceptions
230	}
231	```
232	
233	### Exception Boundary Pattern
234	
235	Use `runCapturingExceptions` to prevent exceptions from unwinding through ORC
236	runtime:
237	
238	```cpp
239	Error safeCallback(std::function<void()> UserCallback) {
240	  return runCapturingExceptions([&]() {
241	    UserCallback();  // User code might throw
242	  });
243	}
244	```
245	
246	### ExceptionError Type
247	
248	`ExceptionError` preserves C++ exceptions as `Error` values:
249	
250	```cpp
251	auto Err = runCapturingExceptions([]() {
252	  throw std::runtime_error("C++ exception");
253	});
254	
255	// Err contains an ExceptionError wrapping the std::runtime_error
256	assert(Err.isA<ExceptionError>());
257	
258	// Can be rethrown with original type preserved
259	Err.throwOnFailure();  // Rethrows std::runtime_error
260	```
261	
262	## Best Practices
263	
264	### 1. Consistent Return Types
265	```cpp
266	// Good: Consistent error handling
267	Expected<Data> loadData(StringRef Path);
268	Error saveData(const Data& D, StringRef Path);
269	
270	// Bad: Mixed error handling
271	Data loadDataOrDie(StringRef Path);  // Inconsistent
272	bool saveData(const Data& D, StringRef Path, std::string* Error);  // C-style
273	```
274	
275	### 2. Meaningful Error Messages
276	```cpp
277	// Good: Descriptive, actionable
278	return make_error<StringError>(
279	  "Failed to parse config file '" + Path + "': invalid JSON at line " +
280	  std::to_string(LineNum)
281	);
282	
283	// Bad: Vague
284	return make_error<StringError>("Parse error");
285	```
286	
287	### 3. Appropriate Error Granularity
288	```cpp
289	// Good: Specific error types enable targeted handling
290	class FileNotFoundError : public ErrorExtends<FileNotFoundError, ErrorInfoBase> {
291	  // ... specific to missing files
292	};
293	
294	class PermissionError : public ErrorExtends<PermissionError, ErrorInfoBase> {
295	  // ... specific to permission issues
296	};
297	
298	// Usage allows specific handling
299	handleAllErrors(openFile(Path),
300	  [](const FileNotFoundError& E) { /* try alternative locations */ },
301	  [](const PermissionError& E)   { /* request elevated access */ },
302	  [](ErrorInfoBase& E)           { /* generic fallback */ }
303	);
304	```
305	
306	### 4. Exception Safety in Mixed Environments
307	```cpp
308	// Safe pattern: Isolate exception-throwing code
309	Error integrateWithExceptionThrowingLibrary() {
310	  return runCapturingExceptions([&]() {
311	    externalLibrary.riskyOperation();
312	    return Error::success();
313	  });
314	}
315	
316	// Unsafe: Exceptions can unwind through Error values
317	Error unsafeIntegration() {
318	  if (auto Err = orcOperation()) {
319	    log("Failed");  // might throw!
320	    return Err;     // ASSERTION FAILURE if log() throws
321	  }
322	  return Error::success();
323	}
324	```
325	
326	### 5. Performance Considerations
327	- `Error::success()` is zero-cost
328	- Avoid creating error objects in hot paths when possible
329	- Use early returns to minimize deep nesting
330	
331	```cpp
332	// Good: Early return, minimal overhead
333	Error fastPath(bool condition) {
334	  if (ORC_RT_LIKELY(condition))
335	    return Error::success();
336	
337	  return make_error<StringError>("Rare error case");
338	}
339	```
340	
341	## Configuration Impact
342	
343	### Exception Disabled (`ORC_RT_ENABLE_EXCEPTIONS=Off`)
344	- `throwOnFailure()` and `runCapturingExceptions()` are not available
345	- `ExceptionError` is not available
346	- All error handling uses `Error`/`Expected<T>` exclusively
347	- Compatible with LLVM projects that disable exceptions
348	
349	### Exceptions Enabled (`ORC_RT_ENABLE_EXCEPTIONS=On`)
350	- Full interoperability between errors and exceptions
351	- Safe integration with exception-throwing external libraries
352	- `ExceptionError` preserves exception values across Error boundaries
353	- Compatible with standard C++ codebases using exceptions
354	
355	## Summary
356	
357	ORC-RT's error handling system provides:
358	
359	- **Type Safety**: Errors have specific types that can be handled appropriately
360	- **Performance**: Zero-cost success path, efficient error propagation
361	- **Flexibility**: Works with or without C++ exceptions
362	- **Interoperability**: Supports integration with exception-throwing code
363	- **Consistency**: Uniform error handling across the entire codebase
364	
365	By following these guidelines, ORC-RT maintains robust error handling that works
366	across diverse integration environments while providing clear, actionable error
367	information to users and developers.
368

# ORC-RT Coding Conventions

## Overview

ORC-RT is part of the LLVM project and generally follows the
[LLVM Coding Standards](https://llvm.org/docs/CodingStandards.html), including
LLVM's naming conventions for C++ code: `PascalCase` for types, values, and
variables, and `camelBack` (lower-camelCase) for functions.

This document records conventions that are specific to ORC-RT, or that need
restating because they are not obvious from the LLVM standards alone. Where this
document is silent, follow the LLVM Coding Standards.

## C API naming

The C API headers (under `include/orc-rt-c/`) cannot use C++ namespaces, so
namespacing is expressed through symbol-name prefixes, while the *casing* of
each name still follows the LLVM naming conventions used elsewhere in the
project.

The rules are:

- **`orc_rt_` is the top-level C namespace.** Every public C symbol begins with
  it.
- **Nested namespaces are additional lower-case, underscore-separated
  segments.** For example, `orc_rt_log_` is the nested namespace for the logging
  API.
- **Types, values, and variables are `PascalCase`** (as in LLVM), appended to
  their namespace prefix.
- **Functions are `camelBack`** (as in LLVM), appended to their namespace
  prefix.
- **Enumerators are `PascalCase` values, scoped by prefixing them with their
  enclosing type's name** (C has no scoped enums), joined with an underscore.
- **Macros are `UPPER_CASE`**, as in LLVM and C generally.

A PascalCase type name may itself act as a scope for its "member" functions,
exactly like a nested namespace does; the two are indistinguishable in the
flattened C name, and both are spelled with a trailing underscore.

### Examples

| Symbol                        | Kind     |
|-------------------------------|----------|
| `orc_rt_ErrorRef`             | type     |
| `orc_rt_Error_getTypeId`      | function |
| `orc_rt_StringError_create`   | function |
| `orc_rt_log_Category`         | type     |
| `orc_rt_log_Category_General` | value    |
| `orc_rt_log_formatCheck`      | function |
| `ORC_RT_LOG`                  | macro    |

Reading these: `orc_rt_Error_getTypeId` is the `getTypeId` function scoped to
the `Error` type; `orc_rt_log_formatCheck` is the `formatCheck` function in the
`log` namespace; and `orc_rt_log_Category_General` is the `General` value of the
`Category` type in the `log` namespace.

## C++ code

C++ code follows the LLVM Coding Standards directly: symbols live in real
namespaces (e.g. `orc_rt`), types/values/variables are `PascalCase`, functions
are `camelBack`, and macros are `UPPER_CASE`.

## Parameter ordering for asynchronous APIs

Many ORC-RT entry points are asynchronous: they take a completion callback that
is invoked, possibly on another thread, when the operation finishes. Because C
has no closures, such a callback is paired with an opaque context (a `void *`
supplied by the caller, or a framework-issued token such as a call id) that is
threaded back to it. To keep these APIs learnable as a family, order their
parameters consistently:

1. The primary handle or receiver (e.g. `orc_rt_SessionRef`) comes first.
2. The call inputs follow (e.g. a target/tag, an argument buffer).
3. The completion callback comes next, immediately followed by its context.
4. The context/token is always **last** -- in both the call and the callback
   signature.

For example, `orc_rt_WrapperFunction` is
`(S, ArgBytes, Return, CallId)` and its return callback
`orc_rt_WrapperFunctionReturn` is `(S, ResultBytes, CallId)`: the `CallId`
token that the framework threads from the call to its completion is last in
both. C++ helpers that mirror these signatures (e.g. `WrapperFunction::handle`)
follow the same order, appending any implementation-only parameters (such as a
serializer or handler) after the token.

This ordering is a convention, not a hard rule; where an existing API or an
external interface being wrapped dictates otherwise, match that instead.

1	//===-------- Service.h - Interface for Session Services --------*- C++ -*-===//
2	//
3	// Part of the LLVM Project, under the Apache License v2.0 with LLVM Exceptions.
4	// See https://llvm.org/LICENSE.txt for license information.
5	// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
6	//
7	//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
8	//
9	// Service class and related APIs.
10	//
11	//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
12	
13	#ifndef ORC_RT_SERVICE_H
14	#define ORC_RT_SERVICE_H
15	
16	#include "orc-rt/Error.h"
17	#include "orc-rt/move_only_function.h"
18	
19	namespace orc_rt {
20	
21	/// A Service typically manages some resource(s) or performs some actions on
22	/// behalf of a Session. E.g. a Memory Manager service.
23	/// Services are owned by the Session and notified when the controller
24	/// detaches, and when the Session shuts down.
25	class Service {
26	public:
27	  using OnCompleteFn = move_only_function<void()>;
28	
29	  virtual ~Service();
30	
31	  /// Called when controller access becomes permanently unavailable.
32	  ///
33	  /// This is guaranteed to be called exactly once before onShutdown,
34	  /// regardless of how the Session reaches that state. It is called when:
35	  ///   - The controller explicitly disconnects.
36	  ///   - The Session::detach() method is called.
37	  ///   - The Session shuts down (even if no controller was ever attached).
38	  ///
39	  /// After onDetach is called no further requests will be made to the Service
40	  /// by the controller. Note that JIT'd code may continue to make requests to
41	  /// the service concurrent with a call to onDetach.
42	  ///
43	  /// If ShutdownRequested is true then a Session shutdown is already pending,
44	  /// and will proceed after all Services have been notified of the detach.
45	  ///
46	  /// onDetach provides an opportunity for Services to release any resources
47	  /// that are only required while the Session is attached to the controller.
48	  /// It is expected that many Services will implement this operation as a
49	  /// no-op.
50	  virtual void onDetach(OnCompleteFn OnComplete, bool ShutdownRequested) = 0;
51	
52	  /// The onShutdown operation will be called at the end of the session.
53	  ///
54	  /// The Service should release any held resources.
55	  virtual void onShutdown(OnCompleteFn OnComplete) = 0;
56	};
57	} // namespace orc_rt
58	
59	#endif // ORC_RT_SERVICE_H

# CMake build for ORC-RT.

#===============================================================================
# Setup Project
#===============================================================================

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20.0)
if("${CMAKE_VERSION}" VERSION_LESS "3.31.0")
  message(WARNING
    "Your CMake version is ${CMAKE_VERSION}. Starting with LLVM 24, the "
    "minimum version of CMake required to build LLVM will become 3.31.0, and "
    "using an older CMake will become an error. Please upgrade your CMake to "
    "at least 3.31.0 now to avoid issues in the future.")
endif()

set(LLVM_COMMON_CMAKE_UTILS ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../cmake)
include(${LLVM_COMMON_CMAKE_UTILS}/Modules/CMakePolicy.cmake
  NO_POLICY_SCOPE)

project(OrcRT LANGUAGES C CXX ASM)

list(INSERT CMAKE_MODULE_PATH 0
  "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/cmake"
  "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/cmake/Modules"
  "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../runtimes/cmake/Modules"
  "${LLVM_COMMON_CMAKE_UTILS}"
  "${LLVM_COMMON_CMAKE_UTILS}/Modules"
  )

include(GNUInstallDirs)

# --- C++ standard ---
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 CACHE STRING "C++ standard to conform to")
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED YES)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS NO)

# --- Project variables ---
set(CMAKE_FOLDER "orc-rt")
set(ORC_RT_SOURCE_DIR ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
set(ORC_RT_BINARY_DIR ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR})

#===============================================================================
# Setup CMake Options
#===============================================================================

# --- Build components ---
option(ORC_RT_INCLUDE_DOCS "Build the ORC-RT documentation." ON)
option(ORC_RT_INCLUDE_TESTS "Build ORC-RT tests." ${LLVM_INCLUDE_TESTS})

# --- Build behavior ---
option(ORC_RT_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS "Enable assertions independent of build mode." ON)
option(ORC_RT_ENABLE_PEDANTIC "Compile with pedantic enabled." ON)
option(ORC_RT_ENABLE_WERROR "Fail and stop if a warning is triggered." OFF)

# --- Language runtime (RTTI / exceptions) ---
option(ORC_RT_ENABLE_RTTI "Enable RTTI." ON)
option(ORC_RT_ENABLE_EXCEPTIONS "Enable exceptions." ON)

# Derive the compile flags implied by the language-runtime options.
set(ORC_RT_COMPILE_FLAGS)
if(ORC_RT_ENABLE_RTTI)
  list(APPEND ORC_RT_COMPILE_FLAGS -frtti)
else()
  list(APPEND ORC_RT_COMPILE_FLAGS -fno-rtti)
endif()

if(ORC_RT_ENABLE_EXCEPTIONS)
  list(APPEND ORC_RT_COMPILE_FLAGS -fexceptions)
else()
  list(APPEND ORC_RT_COMPILE_FLAGS -fno-exceptions)
endif()

# --- Logging ---
# User-settable options (everything below them is validation and derivation):
#   ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND  none (default) | printf | os_log
#   ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL    error | warning | info (default) | debug
set(orc_rt_log_level_default "info")
set(ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL "${orc_rt_log_level_default}" CACHE STRING
  "Lowest log level compiled in: error, warning, info, or debug")
set(orc_rt_log_levels error warning info debug)
set_property(CACHE ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL PROPERTY STRINGS ${orc_rt_log_levels})

set(ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND "none" CACHE STRING
  "ORC-RT logging backend: none, printf, os_log")
set(orc_rt_log_backends none printf os_log)
set_property(CACHE ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND PROPERTY STRINGS ${orc_rt_log_backends})

# Validate the level and derive its config.h macro symbol.
if(NOT ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL IN_LIST orc_rt_log_levels)
  message(FATAL_ERROR "ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL must be one of: ${orc_rt_log_levels}")
endif()
string(TOUPPER "ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_${ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL}" ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_VALUE)

# Validate the backend (os_log is Apple-only) and derive its config.h macro symbol.
if(NOT ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND IN_LIST orc_rt_log_backends)
  message(FATAL_ERROR "ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND must be one of: ${orc_rt_log_backends}")
endif()
if(ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND STREQUAL "os_log" AND NOT APPLE)
  message(FATAL_ERROR "ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND=os_log is only supported on Apple platforms.")
endif()
string(TOUPPER "ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND_${ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND}" ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND_VALUE)

# The "none" backend compiles all logging out, so the level has no effect. Warn
# if the user picked a non-default level under it, as their choice is ignored.
if(ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND STREQUAL "none" AND
   NOT ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL STREQUAL orc_rt_log_level_default)
  message(WARNING
    "ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL is set to '${ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL}', but ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND is "
    "'none', so no logging is compiled in and the level has no effect. Select a "
    "backend (printf or os_log) to enable logging.")
endif()

# --- Generated config header ---
# Keep this last in the section so it captures every value derived above.
configure_file(
  ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include/orc-rt-c/config.h.in
  ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/include/orc-rt-c/config.h
  @ONLY
)

#===============================================================================
# Setup Source Code
#===============================================================================

if (ORC_RT_INCLUDE_DOCS)
  add_subdirectory(docs)
endif()

add_subdirectory(include)
add_subdirectory(lib)
add_subdirectory(tools)

if(ORC_RT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
  add_subdirectory(test)
endif()

9	// Session class and related APIs.
10	//
11	//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
12	
13	#ifndef ORC_RT_SESSION_H
14	#define ORC_RT_SESSION_H
15	
16	#include "orc-rt/BootstrapInfo.h"
17	#include "orc-rt/Error.h"
18	#include "orc-rt/ExecutorProcessInfo.h"
19	#include "orc-rt/LockedAccess.h"
20	#include "orc-rt/Service.h"
21	#include "orc-rt/SimpleSymbolTable.h"
22	#include "orc-rt/TaskGroup.h"
23	#include "orc-rt/WrapperFunction.h"
24	#include "orc-rt/move_only_function.h"
25	
26	#include "orc-rt-c/CoreTypes.h"
27	#include "orc-rt-c/WrapperFunction.h"
28	
29	#include <cassert>
30	#include <condition_variable>
31	#include <memory>
32	#include <mutex>
33	#include <optional>
34	#include <type_traits>
35	#include <vector>
36	
37	namespace orc_rt {
38	class Session;
39	
40	inline orc_rt_SessionRef wrap(Session *S) noexcept {
41	  return reinterpret_cast<orc_rt_SessionRef>(S);
42	}
43	
44	inline Session *unwrap(orc_rt_SessionRef S) noexcept {
45	  return reinterpret_cast<Session *>(S);
46	}
47	
48	/// Represents an ORC executor Session.
49	class Session {
50	private:
51	  // Implementation helper for callManagedCode (non-void version).
52	  template <typename RetT> struct ManagedCodeCaller {
53	    template <typename FnT, typename... ArgTs>
54	    static std::optional<RetT> call(TaskGroup::Token Tok, FnT &&Fn,
55	                                    ArgTs &&...Args) {
56	      if (!Tok)
57	        return std::nullopt;
58	      return std::forward<FnT>(Fn)(std::forward<ArgTs>(Args)...);
59	    }
60	  };
61	
62	  // Implementation helper for callManagedCode (void version).
63	  template <> struct ManagedCodeCaller<void> {
64	    template <typename FnT, typename... ArgTs>
65	    static bool call(TaskGroup::Token Tok, FnT &&Fn, ArgTs &&...Args) {
66	      if (!Tok)
67	        return false;
68	      std::forward<FnT>(Fn)(std::forward<ArgTs>(Args)...);
69	      return true;
70	    }
71	  };
72	
73	public:
74	  using ErrorReporterFn = move_only_function<void(Error)>;
75	  using OnDetachFn = move_only_function<void()>;
76	  using OnShutdownFn = move_only_function<void()>;
77	
78	  /// Return value callback used to return results from callController.
79	  using OnControllerCallReturnFn =
80	      move_only_function<void(WrapperFunctionBuffer)>;
81	
82	  /// A unit of work handed to the Session's DispatchFn for execution.
83	  using Task = move_only_function<void()>;
84	
85	  /// Callback used by the Session to dispatch tasks for execution.
86	  ///
87	  /// The Session builds a Task for each unit of work it needs run -- an
88	  /// incoming wrapper-function call, or a continuation for a result returned
89	  /// by the controller -- and hands it to this callback, which is responsible
90	  /// for arranging the task to be run inline, queued, or posted to a thread
91	  /// pool.
92	  using DispatchFn = move_only_function<void(Task)>;
93	
94	  /// Provides access to the controller.
95	  class ControllerAccess {
96	    friend class Session;
97	
98	  public:
99	    virtual ~ControllerAccess();
100	
101	  protected:
102	    /// Opaque wrapper for a controller-call result handler.
103	    ///
104	    /// ControllerAccess implementations hold these for pending calls but cannot
105	    /// invoke them directly. Each must be completed exactly once, via one of
106	    /// three Session-provided paths, so the handler runs in a context where it
107	    /// may safely touch managed code:
108	    ///
109	    ///   - handleControllerCallResult(OnComplete, ResultBytes): the controller
110	    ///     returned a result. Dispatches the handler under a fresh managed-code
111	    ///     token.
112	    ///
113	    ///   - failPendingControllerCall(OnComplete): a call that was enqueued
114	    ///     while connected is failed because the connection dropped before a
115	    ///     result arrived (the disconnect drain). Dispatches the handler under
116	    ///     a fresh token with a disconnect error.
117	    ///
118	    ///   - failControllerCallInline(OnComplete): a call made from within
119	    ///     callController while already disconnecting, which can therefore
120	    ///     never be enqueued. Runs the handler inline with a disconnect error,
121	    ///     on the caller's stack, covered by the caller's token (see
122	    ///     callController).
123	    ///
124	    /// Together these guarantee the handler always runs exactly once -- with a
125	    /// result or a disconnect error.
126	    class OnControllerCallReturn {
127	      friend class Session;
128	
129	    public:
130	      OnControllerCallReturn() = default;
131	      explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return !!Wrapped; }
132	
133	    private:
134	      OnControllerCallReturn(OnControllerCallReturnFn Wrapped)
135	          : Wrapped(std::move(Wrapped)) {}
136	
137	      OnControllerCallReturnFn Wrapped;
138	    };
139	
140	    ControllerAccess(Session &S) : S(S) {}
141	
142	    /// Initiate connection with controller.
143	    ///
144	    /// This will be called by the Session once it is ready to accept requests
145	    /// from the controller.
146	    ///
147	    /// ControllerAccess implementations must not call handleWrapperCall prior
148	    /// to connect being called.
149	    ///
150	    /// Note: The Session may call into the controller (via callController)
151	    /// during connect, but only in response to a controller-initiated wrapper
152	    /// call. Callers of Session::attach must not race attach with calls to
153	    /// Session::callController.
154	    ///
155	    /// If connect fails to establish communication with the controller,
156	    /// ControllerAccess implementations must call notifyDisconnected before
157	    /// returning from connect.
158	    virtual void connect(BootstrapInfo BI) = 0;
159	
160	    /// Initiate disconnection from the controller.
161	    ///
162	    /// The Session will call this method at most once to request disconnection
163	    /// from the controller. However, disconnection may also be initiated by
164	    /// the controller itself (e.g. a network socket dropping out), potentially
165	    /// concurrently with a Session-initiated disconnect call.
166	    ///
167	    /// ControllerAccess implementations are responsible for handling such
168	    /// double-sided disconnection gracefully, and must ensure that
169	    /// notifyDisconnected is called exactly once regardless of how
170	    /// disconnection occurs. In particular, if the ControllerAccess detects
171	    /// controller-initiated disconnection and calls notifyDisconnected, it
172	    /// must tolerate a subsequent or concurrent call to disconnect (which
173	    /// should be treated as a no-op).
174	    ///
175	    /// notifyDisconnected may be called from within disconnect or
176	    /// asynchronously after disconnect returns. This allows disconnect itself
177	    /// to be a cheap operation (e.g. signaling a shutdown flag) with the
178	    /// actual disconnection and notifyDisconnected call happening on another
179	    /// thread.
180	    ///
181	    /// When disconnecting, a ControllerAccess must fail every still-pending
182	    /// controller call via failPendingControllerCall(OnComplete). This drain
183	    /// must complete before notifyDisconnected, while the managed-code group is
184	    /// still open, so the completions are dispatched rather than dropped
185	    /// (failPendingControllerCall dispatches under a token and asserts the
186	    /// group is open). The drain must be serialized with the disconnecting
187	    /// check in callController, so a call racing disconnection is either
188	    /// drained here or failed inline there -- never left pending.
189	    virtual void disconnect() = 0;
190	
191	    /// Report an error to the session.
192	    void reportError(Error Err) { S.reportError(std::move(Err)); }
193	
194	    /// Call the handler in the controller associated with the given tag.
195	    ///
196	    /// OnComplete must be completed exactly once (see OnControllerCallReturn).
197	    /// On entry, check whether this ControllerAccess has begun disconnecting --
198	    /// its connection state is closing or closed, whether triggered locally by
199	    /// disconnect() or by the remote:
200	    ///
201	    ///   - Still connected: enqueue the continuation. It is later completed via
202	    ///     handleControllerCallResult when the controller returns a result, or
203	    ///     via failPendingControllerCall if disconnection drains it first (see
204	    ///     disconnect).
205	    ///
206	    ///   - Disconnecting: the call can never receive a result, so fail it
207	    ///     immediately via failControllerCallInline, on the current thread.
208	    ///
209	    /// Because the disconnecting case completes the handler inline, the handler
210	    /// may run before callController returns, on the calling thread; callers
211	    /// must tolerate this. It is safe: the caller is still on the stack, so a
212	    /// managed-code caller's token still covers the handler, and a non-managed
213	    /// caller needs none (a handler that re-enters managed code must acquire
214	    /// its own token and handle denial).
215	    virtual void callController(OnControllerCallReturn OnComplete,
216	                                orc_rt_ControllerHandlerTag T,
217	                                WrapperFunctionBuffer ArgBytes) = 0;
218	
219	    /// Send the result of the given wrapper function call to the controller.
220	    virtual void sendWrapperResult(WrapperFunctionBuffer ResultBytes,
221	                                   uint64_t CallId) = 0;
222	
223	    /// Notify the Session that the controller has disconnected.
224	    ///
225	    /// ControllerAccess implementations must call this method exactly once
226	    /// when the controller disconnects, whether initiated by a call to
227	    /// disconnect, by the controller, or by a communication failure.
228	    ///
229	    /// It is the ControllerAccess implementation's responsibility to ensure
230	    /// exactly-once semantics for this method, even when disconnect is called
231	    /// concurrently with controller-initiated disconnection.
232	    ///
233	    /// No calls should be made to reportError, handleWrapperCall, or
234	    /// handleControllerCallResult after this method is called.
235	    void notifyDisconnected() { S.handleDisconnect(); }
236	
237	    /// Ask the Session to run the given wrapper function.
238	    ///
239	    /// Subclasses must not call this method after notifyDisconnected is called.
240	    void handleWrapperCall(orc_rt_WrapperFunction Fn,
241	                           WrapperFunctionBuffer ArgBytes, uint64_t CallId) {
242	      S.handleWrapperCall(Fn, std::move(ArgBytes), CallId);
243	    }
244	
245	    /// Complete a controller call with a result the controller returned, by
246	    /// dispatching its handler under a fresh managed-code token. Must be called
247	    /// while the managed-code group is still open -- i.e. before
248	    /// notifyDisconnected; the Session asserts this.
249	    ///
250	    /// To fail a pending call on disconnect, use failPendingControllerCall.
251	    void handleControllerCallResult(OnControllerCallReturn OnComplete,
252	                                    WrapperFunctionBuffer ResultBytes) {
253	      S.handleControllerCallResult(std::move(OnComplete),
254	                                   std::move(ResultBytes));
255	    }
256	
257	    /// Fail a pending (already-enqueued) controller call because the connection
258	    /// dropped before it received a result -- the disconnect drain.
259	    ///
260	    /// Equivalent to completing it with a disconnect error via
261	    /// handleControllerCallResult (dispatched under a token, same open-group
262	    /// requirement), but named for the drain and taking no result, so the
263	    /// failure value can't be gotten wrong.
264	    void failPendingControllerCall(OnControllerCallReturn OnComplete) {
265	      S.failPendingControllerCall(std::move(OnComplete));
266	    }
267	
268	    /// Fail a controller call by running its handler inline, on the current
269	    /// thread, with a disconnect error -- without acquiring a managed-code
270	    /// token.
271	    ///
272	    /// Use ONLY from within callController, to fail a call that arrives while
273	    /// already disconnecting (see callController). The original caller is then
274	    /// still on the stack, so the handler is covered by the caller's token, or
275	    /// needs none. A call that was successfully enqueued is instead failed via
276	    /// failPendingControllerCall; a real result uses
277	    /// handleControllerCallResult.
278	    void failControllerCallInline(OnControllerCallReturn OnComplete) {
279	      S.failControllerCallInline(std::move(OnComplete));
280	    }
281	
282	  private:
283	    Session &S;
284	  };
285	
286	  /// Create a session object. The ReportError function will be called to
287	  /// report errors generated while serving JIT'd code, e.g. if a memory
288	  /// management request cannot be fulfilled. (Errors within the JIT'd
289	  /// program are not generally visible to ORC-RT, but can optionally be
290	  /// reported by calling the orc_rt_Session_reportError function.)
291	  ///
292	  /// The Dispatch callback is invoked to run tasks generated by the Session
293	  /// (incoming wrapper-function calls, and continuations for results returned
294	  /// by the controller), and is responsible for arranging each task to be run
295	  /// inline, queued, or posted to a thread pool.
296	  ///
297	  /// Note that entry into the reporter is not synchronized: it may be
298	  /// called from multiple threads concurrently.
299	  Session(ExecutorProcessInfo EPI, DispatchFn Dispatch,
300	          ErrorReporterFn ReportError);
301	
302	  // Sessions are not copyable or moveable.
303	  Session(const Session &) = delete;
304	  Session &operator=(const Session &) = delete;
305	  Session(Session &&) = delete;
306	  Session &operator=(Session &&) = delete;
307	
308	  /// Destroy the session object.

<result>## SPS (Simple Packed Serialization) Subsystem Summary

**What is SPS?** Simple Packed Serialization is a binary serialization scheme used in LLVM ORC to serialize/deserialize arguments and return values for cross-process wrapper function calls. It uses a compact format: primitives in little-endian bytes, sequences as length+elements, and tuples as concatenated elements.

**What is sps-ci?** The "Controller Interface" (`sps_ci`) provides registration functions that expose SPS-serialized handlers as symbols in a symbol table, enabling cross-process RPC-style calls between ORC components.

---

### File Summaries

---

#### 1. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SimplePackedSerialization.h`

**Purpose:** Core serialization framework defining buffer types, tag types, and traits for serializing/deserializing values to/from binary blobs.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `SPSOutputBuffer` / `SPSInputBuffer` - Overflow/underflow-checked buffers for writing/reading serialized data
- `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSTagT, ConcreteT>` - Template to specialize for custom serialization behavior
- `SPSArgList<...ArgTs>` - Variadic utility for serializing argument lists
- Tag types: `SPSTuple<...Ts>`, `SPSSequence<T>`, `SPSString`, `SPSOptional<T>`, `SPSMap<K,V>`, `SPSExpected<T>`, `SPSError`

**Connections:** All other SPS files depend on this. Defines the wire format used throughout ORC.

**Concrete Example:** Serializing `int32_t` writes 4 bytes in little-endian order. Serializing `std::vector<int32_t>` writes a `uint64_t` length followed by each int32_t element.

---

#### 2. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SPSWrapperFunction.h`

**Purpose:** Utilities for calling and handling wrapper functions that use SPS to serialize/deserialize their arguments and return values.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `SPSWrapperFunction<SPSSig>` - Main template providing `call()` and `handle()` methods
- `WrapperFunctionSPSSerializer<SPSSig>` - Serializer for function signatures
- `ORC_RT_SPS_WRAPPER(Name, SPSSig, Handle)` - Macro to define SPS wrapper functions

**Connections:** Uses `SimplePackedSerialization.h` and `WrapperFunction.h`. Bridges SPS with the wrapper function call mechanism.

---

#### 3. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SPSWrapperFunctionBuffer.h`

**Purpose:** Specializes SPSSerializationTraits for `WrapperFunctionBuffer`, enabling it to be serialized as (size, data) pairs.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSWrapperFunctionBuffer, WrapperFunctionBuffer>` - Custom trait

**Connections:** Enables nested SPS serialization (buffers containing buffers).

---

#### 4. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SPSMemoryFlags.h`

**Purpose:** SPS serialization for memory-related types, specifically `AllocGroup` which represents memory allocation groups.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSAllocGroup, AllocGroup>` - Serializes AllocGroup as its underlying integer ID

**Connections:** Links memory management types (`MemoryFlags.h`) with SPS.

---

#### 5. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/SPSAllocAction.h`

**Purpose:** Utilities for implementing allocation actions (finalize/deallocate callbacks) that use SPS-serialized arguments.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `ORC_RT_SPS_ALLOC_ACTION(Name, SPSArgs, Handle)` - Macro to define alloc-action wrapper functions
- `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSAllocAction, AllocAction>` - Serializes function pointer + args
- `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSAllocActionPair, AllocActionPair>` - Serializes finalize+dealloc pairs
- `SPSAllocActionFunction<...SPSArgTs>` - Handler template for alloc actions

**Connections:** Uses `AllocAction.h` and SPS. Enables serialization of deferred cleanup operations.

---

#### 6. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/sps-ci/AllSPSCI.h`

**Purpose:** Convenience header that declares `addAll()` to register all SPS controller interface symbols at once.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `orc_rt::sps_ci::addAll(SimpleSymbolTable &ST)` - Registers all interfaces

**Connections:** Aggregates all sps-ci headers (CallSPSCI, MemoryAccessSPSCI, etc.).

---

#### 7. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/sps-ci/CallSPSCI.h`

**Purpose:** Declares registration for function-call-related controller interface symbols (e.g., calling void functions and main).

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `orc_rt::sps_ci::addCall(SimpleSymbolTable &ST)` - Registers call interface symbols

**Connections:** Exposes symbols like `orc_rt_ci_sps_call_void_void` and `orc_rt_ci_sps_call_main`.

---

#### 8. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/include/orc-rt/sps-ci/MemoryAccessSPSCI.h`

**Purpose:** Declares registration for memory access controller interface symbols.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `orc_rt::sps_ci::addMemoryAccess(SimpleSymbolTable &ST)` - Registers memory access symbols

**Connections:** Interfaces with memory mapping/protection operations.

---

#### 9. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/lib/executor/sps-ci/AllSPSCI.cpp`

**Purpose:** Implementation of `sps_ci::addAll()` that calls all individual registration functions.

**Key Types/Classes:**
- Calls `addSimpleNativeMemoryMap` (and potentially others in an array)

**Connections:** Currently only registers the simple native memory map interface.

---

#### 10. `/home/runner/work/codeReader/codeReader/work/llvm-llvm-project/orc-rt/lib/executor/sps-ci/CallSPSCI.cpp`

**Purpose:** Implements and registers function-call handler wrappers for calling void functions and main().

**Key Types/Classes:**
- `call_void_void` - Handler that takes a void function pointer and calls it
- `call_main` - Handler that calls `main(argc, argv)` with string args
- `ORC_RT_SPS_WRAPPER(orc_rt_ci_sps_call_void_void, ...)` - Wrapped void caller
- `ORC_RT_SPS_WRAPPER(orc_rt_ci_sps_call_main, ...)` - Wrapped main caller (signature: `int64_t(SPSExecutorAddr, SPSSequence<SPSString>)`)

**Connections:** Defines concrete cross-process callable functions using `SPSWrapperFunction.h`. Example of how to build an sps-ci handler: define a C++ function, wrap it with `ORC_RT_SPS_WRAPPER`, and add it to a symbol table array.

---

### Serialization Example Summary

To serialize a value:
1. Call `SPSArgList<T>::size(value)` to get required buffer size
2. Create `SPSOutputBuffer` with that size
3. Call `SPSArgList<T>::serialize(OB, value)` to write bytes

To deserialize:
1. Create `SPSInputBuffer` from incoming bytes
2. Call `SPSArgList<T>::deserialize(IB, value)` to read into `value`

For custom types, specialize `SPSSerializationTraits<SPSTagT, ConcreteT>` with `size()`, `serialize()`, and `deserialize()` methods.</result>

## Conceptual Questions Answered

### Relationship between C API (orc-rt-c/) and C++ API (orc_rt namespace)

The C API is a thin ABI boundary layer that provides C-compatible opaque types and functions that wrap the underlying C++ implementation. Key relationships:

1. **Opaque "Ref" types** map to C++ class instances:
   - `orc_rt_SessionRef` → `orc_rt::Session`
   - `orc_rt_ErrorRef` → `llvm::Error` (or subclass)

2. **C functions** typically delegate to C++ methods with type-punning:
   - `orc_rt_Session_callController()` → calls into `Session::callController()`

3. **Purpose:** The C API enables:
   - ABI stability across compiler versions
   - Interoperability with C code
   - Clean boundaries between controller (LLVM JIT) and executor (target code)

### Core C "Ref" Opaque Types

The three fundamental opaque types are:

1. **`orc_rt_ErrorRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueError *`)
   - Null = success, non-null = failure
   - Must be consumed or disposed

2. **`orc_rt_SessionRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueSession *`)
   - Represents the executor's session object
   - Passed to wrapper functions and controller calls

3. **`orc_rt_ControllerHandlerTag`** (`void *`)
   - Identifier for a callable handler in the controller
   - Used as routing key for `callController()`

### InProcessControllerAccess vs Remote Controller

**InProcessControllerAccess** is for when controller and executor share the same process:

- **Mechanism:** Direct function calls through a `Connection` struct with function pointers
- **No serialization:** WrapperFunctionBuffer still used but no IPC overhead
- **Zero-copy:** Data stays in-process, no transport layer
- **Connection:** Handshake via `OnConnect` callback that sets up mutual function pointers

**Remote controller** (not in this codebase, but conceptually):
- **Mechanism:** IPC (shared memory, pipes, network)
- **Serialization:** Full serialization/deserialization required
- **Transport layer:** Explicit message passing
- **Connection:** Socket/pipe establishment

The key architectural point is that `InProcessControllerAccess` implements the same `Session::ControllerAccess` interface but uses function pointers instead of IPC, achieving the same semantic model with better performance for same-process deployment.

### BootstrapInfo Usage

**BootstrapInfo** is the initialization data package passed from executor to controller during connection:

1. **Contains:**
   - `SimpleSymbolTable` - Named addresses (most critically `orc_rt_Session_Instance`)
   - `ValueMap` - String-to-string key/value pairs

2. **Flow:**
   - Created in executor via `BootstrapInfo::CreateDefault()`
   - Passed to `InProcessControllerAccess::connect()`
   - Exposed to controller via `BootstrapInfoAccess` C-ABI interface
   - Controller iterates symbols/values to initialize its `ExecutorProcessControl`

3. **Purpose:** Enables the controller to discover the executor's Session object and platform properties without prior knowledge.

### ExecutorProcessInfo Contents

**ExecutorProcessInfo** holds two critical process properties:

1. **`targetTriple`** (std::string)
   - Example: "x86_64-apple-darwin" or "aarch64-unknown-linux"
   - Derived from architecture/vendor/OS preprocessor macros
   - Tells the controller what platform the executor runs on

2. **`pageSize`** (size_t)
   - System page size from `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)`
   - Must be power-of-2
   - Required for memory allocation and alignment

These properties are immutable after detection and are fundamental to the controller's ability to manage memory in the executor process.</result>

29	/// by a worker thread.

31	/// Lifetime: the runner must outlive the Session that uses it. By the time
32	/// the runner is destroyed the Session must have shut down — operator()
33	/// after destruction begins is a contract violation (asserted). Any tasks
34	/// already pending in the queue at destruction time will be drained by the
35	/// workers before they exit.

### Relationship between C API (orc-rt-c/) and C++ API (orc_rt namespace)

The C API is a thin ABI boundary layer that provides C-compatible opaque types and functions that wrap the underlying C++ implementation. Key relationships:

1. **Opaque "Ref" types** map to C++ class instances:
   - `orc_rt_SessionRef` → `orc_rt::Session`
   - `orc_rt_ErrorRef` → `llvm::Error` (or subclass)

2. **C functions** typically delegate to C++ methods with type-punning:
   - `orc_rt_Session_callController()` → calls into `Session::callController()`

3. **Purpose:** The C API enables:
   - ABI stability across compiler versions
   - Interoperability with C code
   - Clean boundaries between controller (LLVM JIT) and executor (target code)

### Core C "Ref" Opaque Types

The three fundamental opaque types are:

1. **`orc_rt_ErrorRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueError *`)
   - Null = success, non-null = failure
   - Must be consumed or disposed

2. **`orc_rt_SessionRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueSession *`)
   - Represents the executor's session object
   - Passed to wrapper functions and controller calls

3. **`orc_rt_ControllerHandlerTag`** (`void *`)
   - Identifier for a callable handler in the controller
   - Used as routing key for `callController()`

### InProcessControllerAccess vs Remote Controller

**InProcessControllerAccess** is for when controller and executor share the same process:

- **Mechanism:** Direct function calls through a `Connection` struct with function pointers
- **No serialization:** WrapperFunctionBuffer still used but no IPC overhead
- **Zero-copy:** Data stays in-process, no transport layer
- **Connection:** Handshake via `OnConnect` callback that sets up mutual function pointers

**Remote controller** (not in this codebase, but conceptually):
- **Mechanism:** IPC (shared memory, pipes, network)
- **Serialization:** Full serialization/deserialization required
- **Transport layer:** Explicit message passing
- **Connection:** Socket/pipe establishment

The key architectural point is that `InProcessControllerAccess` implements the same `Session::ControllerAccess` interface but uses function pointers instead of IPC, achieving the same semantic model with better performance for same-process deployment.

### BootstrapInfo Usage

**BootstrapInfo** is the initialization data package passed from executor to controller during connection:

1. **Contains:**
   - `SimpleSymbolTable` - Named addresses (most critically `orc_rt_Session_Instance`)
   - `ValueMap` - String-to-string key/value pairs

2. **Flow:**
   - Created in executor via `BootstrapInfo::CreateDefault()`
   - Passed to `InProcessControllerAccess::connect()`
   - Exposed to controller via `BootstrapInfoAccess` C-ABI interface
   - Controller iterates symbols/values to initialize its `ExecutorProcessControl`

3. **Purpose:** Enables the controller to discover the executor's Session object and platform properties without prior knowledge.

### ExecutorProcessInfo Contents

**ExecutorProcessInfo** holds two critical process properties:

1. **`targetTriple`** (std::string)
   - Example: "x86_64-apple-darwin" or "aarch64-unknown-linux"
   - Derived from architecture/vendor/OS preprocessor macros
   - Tells the controller what platform the executor runs on

2. **`pageSize`** (size_t)
   - System page size from `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)`
   - Must be power-of-2
   - Required for memory allocation and alignment

These properties are immutable after detection and are fundamental to the controller's ability to manage memory in the executor process.</result>

### Relationship between C API (orc-rt-c/) and C++ API (orc_rt namespace)

The C API is a thin ABI boundary layer that provides C-compatible opaque types and functions that wrap the underlying C++ implementation. Key relationships:

1. **Opaque "Ref" types** map to C++ class instances:
   - `orc_rt_SessionRef` → `orc_rt::Session`
   - `orc_rt_ErrorRef` → `llvm::Error` (or subclass)

2. **C functions** typically delegate to C++ methods with type-punning:
   - `orc_rt_Session_callController()` → calls into `Session::callController()`

3. **Purpose:** The C API enables:
   - ABI stability across compiler versions
   - Interoperability with C code
   - Clean boundaries between controller (LLVM JIT) and executor (target code)

### Core C "Ref" Opaque Types

The three fundamental opaque types are:

1. **`orc_rt_ErrorRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueError *`)
   - Null = success, non-null = failure
   - Must be consumed or disposed

2. **`orc_rt_SessionRef`** (`struct orc_rt_OpaqueSession *`)
   - Represents the executor's session object
   - Passed to wrapper functions and controller calls

3. **`orc_rt_ControllerHandlerTag`** (`void *`)
   - Identifier for a callable handler in the controller
   - Used as routing key for `callController()`

### InProcessControllerAccess vs Remote Controller

**InProcessControllerAccess** is for when controller and executor share the same process:

- **Mechanism:** Direct function calls through a `Connection` struct with function pointers
- **No serialization:** WrapperFunctionBuffer still used but no IPC overhead
- **Zero-copy:** Data stays in-process, no transport layer
- **Connection:** Handshake via `OnConnect` callback that sets up mutual function pointers

**Remote controller** (not in this codebase, but conceptually):
- **Mechanism:** IPC (shared memory, pipes, network)
- **Serialization:** Full serialization/deserialization required
- **Transport layer:** Explicit message passing
- **Connection:** Socket/pipe establishment

The key architectural point is that `InProcessControllerAccess` implements the same `Session::ControllerAccess` interface but uses function pointers instead of IPC, achieving the same semantic model with better performance for same-process deployment.

### BootstrapInfo Usage

**BootstrapInfo** is the initialization data package passed from executor to controller during connection:

1. **Contains:**
   - `SimpleSymbolTable` - Named addresses (most critically `orc_rt_Session_Instance`)
   - `ValueMap` - String-to-string key/value pairs

2. **Flow:**
   - Created in executor via `BootstrapInfo::CreateDefault()`
   - Passed to `InProcessControllerAccess::connect()`
   - Exposed to controller via `BootstrapInfoAccess` C-ABI interface
   - Controller iterates symbols/values to initialize its `ExecutorProcessControl`

3. **Purpose:** Enables the controller to discover the executor's Session object and platform properties without prior knowledge.

### ExecutorProcessInfo Contents

**ExecutorProcessInfo** holds two critical process properties:

1. **`targetTriple`** (std::string)
   - Example: "x86_64-apple-darwin" or "aarch64-unknown-linux"
   - Derived from architecture/vendor/OS preprocessor macros
   - Tells the controller what platform the executor runs on

2. **`pageSize`** (size_t)
   - System page size from `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)`
   - Must be power-of-2
   - Required for memory allocation and alignment

These properties are immutable after detection and are fundamental to the controller's ability to manage memory in the executor process.</result>

79	/**

81	 * unrecognized.
82	 */

88	 * is unrecognized.

91	
92	/**
93	 * Returns the level corresponding to the given level name, or -1 if the level
94	 * name is unrecognized.
95	 *
96	 * Comparison is case-insensitive.
97	 */
98	orc_rt_log_Level orc_rt_log_Level_parse(const char *Str) ORC_RT_C_NOTHROW;
99	
100	/*
101	 * Declared but never defined: referenced only in unevaluated (sizeof) contexts
102	 * to type-check a printf-style format string against its arguments without
103	 * evaluating them or emitting any code.
104	 */
105	int orc_rt_log_formatCheck(const char *Fmt, ...) ORC_RT_C_FORMAT_PRINTF(1, 2);
106	
107	/*
108	 * A disabled log site. Validates the category token, format string, and
109	 * arguments at compile time, but evaluates nothing and generates no code:
110	 * both operands sit in unevaluated sizeof contexts.
111	 */
112	#define ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, ...)                                     \
113	  ((void)sizeof(Category), (void)sizeof(orc_rt_log_formatCheck(__VA_ARGS__)))
114	
115	/*
116	 * ORC_RT_LOG dispatches on the level token to a per-level macro, which each
117	 * backend defines below to either emit a message or, when the level is
118	 * compiled out, to ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED. Fmt is the first variadic argument, so
119	 * __VA_ARGS__ is always non-empty and no GNU comma-swallowing extension is
120	 * needed.
121	 *
122	 * The leading (void)sizeof("" __VA_ARGS__, 0) requires Fmt to be a string
123	 * literal on every backend. The os_log backend needs a literal regardless (it
124	 * builds format metadata at the call site), and enforcing it uniformly stops a
125	 * non-literal format from compiling on the none/printf backends only to break
126	 * an os_log build. It is unevaluated, so it emits no code and does not evaluate
127	 * the arguments; the trailing ", 0" keeps sizeof's operand a scalar (avoiding
128	 * -Wsizeof-array-decay). A non-literal Fmt produces a syntax error here.
129	 */
130	#define ORC_RT_LOG(Level, Category, ...)                                       \
131	  ((void)sizeof("" __VA_ARGS__, 0),                                            \
132	   ORC_RT_LOG_##Level(orc_rt_log_Category_##Category, __VA_ARGS__))
133	
134	/**
135	 * \def ORC_RT_LOG_PUB_S
136	 * Conversion specifier for publishing a runtime (non-literal) C string.
137	 *
138	 * Use this in place of a plain "%s" whenever you are logging a runtime string
139	 * that should be readable in the log output: on os_log a "%s" argument defaults
140	 * to private and is redacted in the system log, so ORC_RT_LOG_PUB_S is what

142	 * plain "%s" (which stays private) for anything a sandboxed or privacy-
143	 * sensitive deployment should not disclose, or do not log it at all. The printf
144	 * backend has no public/private distinction and always prints the string
145	 * regardless.

148	 * runtime string differs by backend, so it cannot be written inline. This
149	 * macro expands to a string literal that the surrounding format is expected to
150	 * concatenate by literal adjacency, e.g.
151	 *
152	 *   ORC_RT_LOG(Info, General, "resolved " ORC_RT_LOG_PUB_S, SymbolName);

154	 * keeping Fmt a single literal on every backend.
155	 *

164	#endif

166	#if ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND == ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND_NONE
167	
168	/* The none backend compiles every level out, regardless of ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL. */
169	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Error(Category, ...)                                        \
170	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
171	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Warning(Category, ...)                                      \
172	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
173	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Info(Category, ...)                                         \
174	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
175	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Debug(Category, ...)                                        \

177	
178	#elif ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND == ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND_PRINTF
179	
180	/*
181	 * printf-backend log sink. Formats the message and writes it, prefixed with its
182	 * category and level, to the logging output (stderr, or the file named by the
183	 * ORC_RT_LOG_OUTPUT environment variable). Not called directly: use ORC_RT_LOG.
184	 */
185	void orc_rt_log_printf(orc_rt_log_Level Level, orc_rt_log_Category Category,
186	                       const char *Fmt, ...) ORC_RT_C_NOTHROW
187	    ORC_RT_C_FORMAT_PRINTF(3, 4);

191	 * floor; a below-floor level expands to ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED so it
192	 * vanishes from the binary while remaining type-checked.
193	 */
194	#if ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_ERROR >= ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL

196	  orc_rt_log_printf(ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_ERROR, Category, __VA_ARGS__)

198	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Error(Category, ...)                                        \
199	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
200	#endif
201	
202	#if ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_WARNING >= ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL
203	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Warning(Category, ...)                                      \
204	  orc_rt_log_printf(ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_WARNING, Category, __VA_ARGS__)
205	#else
206	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Warning(Category, ...)                                      \
207	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
208	#endif

210	#if ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_INFO >= ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL
211	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Info(Category, ...)                                         \
212	  orc_rt_log_printf(ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_INFO, Category, __VA_ARGS__)
213	#else
214	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Info(Category, ...)                                         \
215	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
216	#endif
217	
218	#if ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG >= ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL
219	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Debug(Category, ...)                                        \
220	  orc_rt_log_printf(ORC_RT_LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG, Category, __VA_ARGS__)
221	#else
222	#define ORC_RT_LOG_Debug(Category, ...)                                        \
223	  ORC_RT_LOG_DISABLED(Category, __VA_ARGS__)
224	#endif

226	#elif ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND == ORC_RT_LOG_BACKEND_OS_LOG

229	 * Per-category os_log_t cache, homed in Logging_oslog.cpp. Slots start null and
230	 * are filled lazily (and read) atomically by orc_rt_log_osLogHandle. An
231	 * implementation detail of that accessor; do not use directly.
232	 */

241	orc_rt_log_osLogHandleSlow(orc_rt_log_Category Category) ORC_RT_C_NOTHROW;

246	 * check stays cheap; the warm path is just an atomic load. Returns
